sub1: Weeks 17-18 Swapped re-ordered by hand to cut fatigue — same duties, same days, same coverage; only which week sits next to which has changed
sub3: What this design keeps of today, and where the December headcounts differ
coverNote: gaps of 7, 6, 5, 6 around the wheel — close to even, one line out; unchanged from the design this re-orders
sub7: Checkable rather than reproducible: there is no search behind it, and every figure is computed from the cells
method:
1 · It was re-ordered by hand, not searched. This rotation arrived as a Word table describing a series of named, deliberate moves against Weeks 17-18 Swapped — a same-day duty swap at a time, each one argued in the document. It was read straight into the app's own shape and judged; no grid was annealed, so there is no search to reproduce. What can be reproduced is every figure on these pages.

2 · The document's central claim was tested first, and it holds. It states that every duty moved stays on the SAME weekday, so the number and type of shifts available on each day are preserved. Checked against Weeks 17-18 Swapped: each day's multiset of duties is identical, and so is the hour-by-hour coverage curve — every quarter-hour of the whole week. Nothing was invented, nothing re-timed, and no day lost or gained a person.

3 · The reading was checksummed before anything was built on it. A grid read from a document can carry a silent transcription error, so the duty minutes were totalled against the contract first: Monday to Saturday comes to 42,000 minutes against 20 working lines × 35h = 42,000, exactly. Every one of the document's own 24 stated weekly totals also matches its cells to the minute.

4 · The judge is the workspace's own — runDesignChecks, weeklyHours, assessHardLimits, assessFatigue, scoreOrder and calcHourlyCoverage, with nothing typed by hand and nothing softened. Where the design misses one of the December rules the table opposite says so rather than omitting the row.
openQuestions: One of the two targets was hit outright; the other depends on how a cover week is worked. The document sets out to clear two flags. The first is cleared on any reading: the worst seven-day total falls from 60.6 hours to 54.7, under the 55-hour row, and the document's own estimate of “about 54h40” is right. The second is the interesting one. It reports the run “dropping from about 15 duties to 9”, and there are three different measures in that sentence. 9 is the longest run of consecutive worked DAYS — correct, and inside Chiltern's thirteen. FF11 counts shifts between 48-hour breaks, and a single rest day is not one. On that measure this design is at 15 in the worst case, down from 16 and over the threshold of 13 — but 12 as rostered, under it. The difference is entirely the cover week: the 15 needs one split day-on-day-off so that it supplies no break and joins the blocks either side, and a cover week worked as a block always supplies one. So whether this design clears FF11 is a question for the roster office, not for the link, and page 6 prints both. What the re-ordering cost. Factors present fall from five to four in the worst case (three as rostered), but not uniformly: FF19 rises from 7 to 8, full weekends off fall from 6 to 5, and single-turn weeks fall from 6 of 20 to 4, so more weeks now ask somebody to hold more than one start time. Every hard gate stays clear — 35h to the minute, no rest under 12 hours, no hard-limit breach, longest run nine days inside the thirteen on either reading. The unfinished question is the same one the design it re-orders left open. None of what remains needs a duty to change: FF11, FF15, FF8b and FF19 are all properties of which week sits next to which. On this exact duty table, the same shape work done by the workspace's own search takes the factors to one and the run to six or seven with the coverage curve untouched — the three searched proposals opposite are that result. This one is listed as supplied, deliberately, so the hand-made baseline stays on the record.
